syllabusAlert: Syllabus Sync: Zero deletions across NTA JEE Mains, NMC NEET UG, and IIT JEE Advanced. SI units, dimensional homogeneity, significant figures, error propagation, Vernier Callipers, Screw Gauge, Meter Bridge, Resonance Tube, Optical Bench, Searle's Apparatus & Ohm's Law setup are all retained.

sections.heading: SI Base Units, Dimensional Homogeneity & Application Boundaries
sections.summary: The SI framework expresses every physical observable in terms of seven fundamental base dimensions: [M], [L], [T], [I/A], [K], [mol], and [cd]. Dimensional homogeneity requires that every additive or subtractive term across an equation carry identical net exponents, enabling instant formula verification and conversion between unit systems.
keyPoints: Seven SI base quantities and symbols: Mass (kg, [M]), Length (m, [L]), Time (s, [T]), Electric Current (A, [I] or [A]), Thermodynamic Temperature (K, [K]), Amount of Substance (mol, [mol]), Luminous Intensity (cd, [cd]). Supplementary plane angle (rad) and solid angle (sr) carry units but zero dimensions.

Transcendental & ratio rule: Arguments of sin(x), cos(x), tan(x), exp(x), ln(x), and ratios such as strain, relative density, refractive index, coefficient of friction, and dielectric constant K are strictly dimensionless [M^0 L^0 T^0].

High-yield identical-dimension groups: (a) Work, Energy, Torque, Moment of Force: [M L^2 T^(-2)]; (b) Pressure, Stress, Young's/Bulk/Shear Modulus, Energy Density (1/2)eps_0 E^2 = B^2/(2 mu_0): [M L^(-1) T^(-2)]; (c) Planck's constant h and Angular Momentum L: [M L^2 T^(-1)].

Electrical & thermal benchmark dimensions: Permittivity eps_0 = [M^(-1) L^(-3) T^4 A^2]; Permeability mu_0 = [M L T^(-2) A^(-2)]; Time constants RC = L/R = sqrt(LC) = [T]; Stefan constant sigma = [M T^(-3) K^(-4)]; Universal gas constant R = [M L^2 T^(-2) K^(-1) mol^(-1)].

Unit conversion scaling: Since n1 u1 = n2 u2, changing base units yields n2 = n1 (M1/M2)^a (L1/L2)^b (T1/T2)^c. Using [c], [G], [h] as base units gives Planck Length l_P = sqrt(h_bar G / c^3) ~ 1.6 x 10^(-35) m and Planck Mass sqrt(h_bar c / G).

Fundamental limits of dimensional analysis: Cannot determine dimensionless numerical constants (e.g., 1/2, 2 pi), fails for sums/differences of terms (s = ut + 1/2 at^2), fails when a quantity depends on more than 3 independent mechanical variables, and cannot distinguish scalars from vectors (Torque vs Work).

sections.heading: Significant Figures, Rounding Rules & Limiting Error Propagation
sections.summary: Significant figures encode the reliable precision of an experimental measurement up to its first uncertain digit. Error calculus combines independent uncertainties conservatively so that maximum possible error always bounds the worst-case deviation in derived quantities.
keyPoints: Significant figure counting rules: All non-zero digits and trapped zeros (3004 -> 4 SF) are significant. Leading zeros (0.0042 -> 2 SF) are NEVER significant. Trailing zeros after a decimal point ARE significant (4.200 -> 4 SF), while trailing zeros in whole numbers without a decimal point are non-significant unless written in scientific notation (4.20 x 10^3 -> 3 SF).
Exact numbers & constants: Pure counting integers (2 in 2 pi r) and mathematical constants (pi, e) carry infinite significant figures and NEVER restrict final SF rounding.

Arithmetic rounding convention: In addition/subtraction, round result to the LEAST number of decimal places among operands (e.g., 12.11 + 18.0 -> 30.1). In multiplication/division, round to the LEAST number of significant figures among operands.

Rounding off digit 5 rule (Banker's / NCERT): If digit to drop is > 5, increment preceding digit by 1; if < 5, leave unchanged; if exactly 5 followed by non-zeros, increment; if exactly 5 followed only by zeros (or nothing), increment ONLY if preceding digit is ODD (leave unchanged if EVEN).

Addition & subtraction error (Z = A + B or Z = A - B): Maximum absolute error ALWAYS ADDS: dZ = dA + dB. Subtracting errors is a classic negative-marking blunder because A and B can deviate in opposite directions simultaneously.

Product, quotient & power error (Z = k A^p B^q / C^r): Maximum fractional error dZ/Z = |p|(dA/A) + |q|(dB/B) + |r|(dC/C), and percentage error %Z = 100 x (dZ/Z). Note that if standard/random errors are given instead of maximum limiting errors, they add in quadrature: sqrt((p dA/A)^2 + ...).

sections.heading: Unit 20 Mechanical Instruments: Vernier Callipers, Screw Gauge & Spherometer
sections.summary: Vernier Callipers and Micrometer Screw Gauges subdivide main-scale ticks using a secondary sliding or rotating scale to achieve sub-millimetre least counts. Every observed reading must have the signed zero error algebraically subtracted to recover the true physical dimension.
keyPoints: Vernier Callipers Least Count (LC): LC = 1 MSD - 1 VSD. When n VSD coincide with m MSD (typically m = n - 1), 1 VSD = (m/n) MSD, giving LC = (1 - m/n) MSD. Standard 10 VSD = 9 MSD with 1 MSD = 1 mm gives LC = 0.1 mm = 0.01 cm.

Non-standard Vernier trap: If n VSD coincide with (n + 1) MSD (extended Vernier), 1 VSD > 1 MSD, so reading uses LC = 1 VSD - 1 MSD or formula N_MSD + (n_coinciding x (1 MSD - 1 VSD)) carefully from first principles of coinciding mark alignment.

Vernier Zero Error convention: Observed = MSR + (VSR x LC). Positive zero error (+e): Vernier 0 sits to the RIGHT of Main 0 -> +e = +k x LC. Negative zero error (-e): Vernier 0 sits to the LEFT of Main 0 -> -e = -(n - k) x LC (subtract from 0, NOT -k x LC!). True Reading = Observed - (Zero Error).

Screw Gauge / Micrometer: Pitch p = linear advance per full rotation = (Distance moved in N rotations) / N. LC = Pitch / N_CSD (number of circular scale divisions). Standard: p = 0.5 mm, N_CSD = 50 -> LC = 0.01 mm = 0.001 cm.

Screw Gauge Zero Error & Backlash: If circular scale zero lies BELOW the horizontal reference line when jaws touch, zero error is POSITIVE (+k x LC). If circular scale zero lies ABOVE the reference line, zero error is NEGATIVE (-(N_CSD - k) x LC). Always rotate ratchet in one direction to avoid backlash error.

Spherometer for radius of curvature R: R = l^2 / (6 h) + h / 2, where l is the average spacing between the three outer legs (equilateral triangle) and h is the central sagitta measured via pitch and circular scale.

sections.heading: Unit 20 Electrical & Acoustic Lab Apparatus: Meter Bridge, Ohm's Law & Resonance Tube
sections.summary: Wheatstone-based null methods eliminate galvanometer resistance and source EMF fluctuations from resistance measurements, while the resonance air column eliminates unknown end correction by differencing two successive resonant lengths. Ohm's Law verification extracts resistance from the linear V-I slope while minimizing Joule heating drift.
keyPoints: Meter Bridge (100 cm Manganin/Constantan wire): Balanced null point at length l gives X / R = l / (100 - l). Manganin/Constantan is chosen for high resistivity and near-zero temperature coefficient alpha.

Meter Bridge end corrections & optimal null point: Contact resistances at thick copper strips shift effective wire ends by alpha (left) and beta (right): X / R = (l + alpha) / (100 - l + beta). Fractional error dX/X is MINIMIZED when l = 50 cm (midpoint), because dX/X = dl * [1/l + 1/(100-l)] minimizes at l = 50 cm.

Interchanging X and R in Meter Bridge: If null shifts from l1 to l2 on swapping X and R (or adding shunt/series R), solve the two simultaneous ratios to eliminate end corrections alpha and beta cleanly.

Ohm's Law V-I experiment: Plot V on y-axis vs I on x-axis; slope dV/dI = R. If plotted I vs V, slope = 1/R. Use low current briefly to avoid heating (which increases R of metallic wire and curves V-I upward). Ammeter (low R) goes in series; Voltmeter (high R) goes in parallel across unknown R.

Resonance Tube (closed at water end): First resonance at L1 + e = lambda/4, second resonance at L2 + e = 3 lambda/4. Subtracting eliminates end correction e: lambda/2 = L2 - L1 => speed of sound v = 2 f (L2 - L1).
End correction formula for cylindrical tube of radius r: e = (L2 - 3 L1) / 2 ~ 0.6 r (typically L2 slightly exceeds 3 L1!). For third resonance L3 + e = 5 lambda/4.

sections.heading: Unit 20 Optical Bench, Travelling Microscope, Searle's Apparatus & Simple Pendulum
sections.summary: Optical bench focal-length determination and travelling-microscope refractive-index experiments rely on parallax-free pin alignment and apparent depth ratios, whereas Searle's apparatus and simple pendulum experiments yield Young's modulus and g via high-precision differential measurements.
keyPoints: Optical Bench (1/f = 1/v - 1/u for convex lens; 1/f = 1/v + 1/u for concave mirror): Remove parallax between inverted real image and image pin by moving eye sideways until both stay aligned. Index correction e = (True distance between pole & pin) - (Bench scale reading).

1/u vs 1/v and u-v graphical checks: Plotting 1/v vs 1/u gives straight line with slope -1 and intercepts 1/f on both axes (lens with Cartesian u < 0, v > 0 plotted as |1/v| vs |1/u| has slope -1 and intercepts 1/f). Minimum distance between real object and real image for convex lens is 4 f.

Travelling Microscope refractive index: Focus on mark at bottom of beaker (reading R1), place glass slab / liquid and refocus on apparent mark (R2), sprinkle lycopodium powder on top surface and focus (R3). Then mu = Real Depth / Apparent Depth = (R3 - R1) / (R3 - R2).

Searle's apparatus for Young's Modulus Y: Uses two identical wires (reference + test) attached to a spirit level frame so temperature fluctuations and support yield cancel automatically! Measure extension dL via micrometer screw gauge for load increments Mg -> Y = (Mg L) / (pi r^2 dL).

Simple Pendulum g measurement: T = 2 pi sqrt(L / g) => g = 4 pi^2 L / T^2. Timing N oscillations (say N = 20) with stopwatch of least count dT reduces error in T to dT_single / N, so % error in g is dL/L + 2 (dT_stopwatch / T_total).

Plotting L vs T^2 for simple pendulum: Gives a straight line passing through origin with slope = g / (4 pi^2). Measuring L from suspension hook to bob centre (L = l_string + r_bob) avoids systematic offset error.

derivationsAndGraphs.title: Meter Bridge Fractional Error Minimization Curve
derivationsAndGraphs.expressionOrCurve: dX/X = [100 / (l (100 - l))] * dl  (U-shaped symmetric curve with minimum at l = 50 cm)
derivationsAndGraphs.keyTakeaway: Since X = R * l/(100-l), differentiating ln X gives dX/X = dl/l + dl/(100-l). Minimum uncertainty occurs strictly at l = 50 cm where dX/X = dl / 25.

derivationsAndGraphs.title: Resonance Air Column End-Correction Cancellation
derivationsAndGraphs.expressionOrCurve: L1 + e = lambda/4 ; L2 + e = 3 lambda/4  =>  v = 2 f (L2 - L1) and e = (L2 - 3 L1)/2
derivationsAndGraphs.keyTakeaway: Antinode forms slightly outside the open mouth at distance e ~ 0.6 r. Comparing L2 against 3 L1 immediately determines whether e is physically positive (~few mm).

derivationsAndGraphs.title: 1/|v| vs 1/|u| Graph for Convex Lens (Real Image)
derivationsAndGraphs.expressionOrCurve: 1/|v| + 1/|u| = 1/f  (Straight line with slope = -1, x-intercept = 1/f, y-intercept = 1/f)
derivationsAndGraphs.keyTakeaway: At |u| = |v| = 2f, the line intersects the y = x symmetry line at (1/2f, 1/2f), giving f = 1 / (2 * intercept_on_45deg_line).

derivationsAndGraphs.title: Pendulum L vs T^2 Linear Regression & Percentage Error
derivationsAndGraphs.expressionOrCurve: L = (g / 4 pi^2) * T^2  ;  (dg / g) = (dL / L) + 2 * (dt / t_total)
derivationsAndGraphs.keyTakeaway: In T = t_total / N, timing N oscillations multiplies total time t_total by N while keeping stopwatch least count dt fixed, cutting time error by factor N.

traps: Subtracting errors in Z = A - B: Whether Z = A + B or Z = A - B, maximum absolute error is ALWAYS dZ = dA + dB.

Negative zero error blunder: On a 50-division screw gauge (LC = 0.01 mm), if the 46th division aligns with the datum line and 0 is slightly ABOVE it, zero error is -(50 - 46) x 0.01 = -0.04 mm (NOT -0.46 mm!).
Extended Vernier trap: When 10 VSD = 11 MSD, 1 VSD = 1.1 MSD. Do NOT blindly apply LC = (1 MSD)/n! Check alignment geometrically.
Percentage error for >5% changes: Differential formula dZ/Z = p(dA/A) applies ONLY to small fractional errors (<~5%). For a 20% or 50% change in A, compute exact ratio [(A_new/A)^p - 1] x 100%!

Least count vs human reaction error: If a question gives 'least count of scale is 0.1 cm' without explicit +/- error, take dL = 0.1 cm (1 LC) as the limiting reading uncertainty unless stated as +/- 0.05 cm.
Dimensional disguise pairs: Energy Density = Pressure = Bulk Modulus; Surface Tension = Spring Constant k; Planck h = Angular Momentum L; Latent Heat = (Velocity)^2 = Gravitational Potential.

solvedExamples.question: A student measures length l = (10.0 +/- 0.1) cm and breadth b = (5.0 +/- 0.1) cm of a rectangular plate. Find the perimeter P = 2(l + b) and area A = l * b with maximum limiting errors and proper significant figures.
steps: Compute nominal perimeter: P = 2(10.0 + 5.0) = 30.0 cm.
Error in perimeter: dP = 2(dl + db) = 2(0.1 + 0.1) = 0.4 cm, so P = (30.0 +/- 0.4) cm.
Compute nominal area: A = 10.0 x 5.0 = 50 cm^2 (rounded to 2 SF since 5.0 has 2 SF).
Fractional error in area: dA/A = dl/l + db/b = 0.1/10.0 + 0.1/5.0 = 0.01 + 0.02 = 0.03.
Absolute error dA = 0.03 x 50 = 1.5 cm^2 (or 2 cm^2 rounded to match precision) -> A = (50.0 +/- 1.5) cm^2.
solvedExamples.pitfall: Forgetting the factor of 2 in dP = 2(dl + db), or writing dA = dl * db = 0.01 cm^2.

solvedExamples.question: In a non-standard Vernier Callipers, 1 MSD = 1 mm and 10 VSD coincide with 8 MSD. When jaws are closed, Vernier 0 lies left of Main 0 and the 6th VSD coincides with a main-scale mark. While measuring a cylinder, MSR = 2.4 cm and 5th VSD coincides. Find true diameter.
steps: Find Least Count: 10 VSD = 8 MSD => 1 VSD = 0.8 mm => LC = 1 MSD - 1 VSD = 1 - 0.8 = 0.2 mm = 0.02 cm.
Compute negative zero error: Since 0 is left of MS 0, e = -(n - k) * LC = -(10 - 6) x 0.2 mm = -0.8 mm = -0.08 cm.
Compute observed reading: Obs = 2.4 cm + 5 x 0.02 cm = 2.50 cm.
Apply zero error correction: True = Obs - e = 2.50 - (-0.08) = 2.58 cm.
solvedExamples.pitfall: Assuming LC = 0.1 mm without checking 10 VSD = 8 MSD, or using e = -6 x 0.2 = -1.2 mm.

solvedExamples.question: A physical quantity X is given by X = (A^2 B^(1/2)) / (C^(1/3) D^3). If percentage errors in A, B, C, and D are 1%, 2%, 3%, and 4% respectively, find the maximum percentage error in X.
steps: Write fractional error rule: dX/X = 2(dA/A) + (1/2)(dB/B) + (1/3)(dC/C) + 3(dD/D).
Multiply throughout by 100 to convert to percentage error.
solvedExamples.pitfall: Subtracting the denominator terms C and D (-1/3 and -3) instead of adding their absolute exponents!

solvedExamples.question: In a resonance tube experiment with a 512 Hz tuning fork, first and second resonances occur at water-level readings L1 = 16.0 cm and L2 = 50.0 cm (each measured with least count 0.1 cm). Find the speed of sound v with its maximum percentage error, and compute the tube's end correction e.
steps: Find error in (L2 - L1): Since it is a difference, errors ADD: d(L2 - L1) = dL2 + dL1 = 0.1 + 0.1 = 0.2 cm.
Compute % error in v (assuming f exact): %v = [d(L2 - L1) / (L2 - L1)] x 100 = (0.2 / 34.0) x 100 = 0.588% ~ 0.59%.
solvedExamples.pitfall: Using d(L2 - L1) = 0.1 - 0.1 = 0 cm! Difference measurements ALWAYS double the single-reading least count error.

weightageNote: Weightage: 4-6% (1-2 questions in JEE Mains & NEET UG; 1 tricky inclined-bounce or relative-geometry problem in JEE Advanced).
syllabusAlert: Syllabus Sync: Scalar & vector kinematics, calculus 1D motion, motion graphs, horizontal & inclined projectiles, and relative velocity (river-boat, rain-man, closest approach) are 100% retained.

sections.heading: 1D Kinematics, Calculus Formulations & Sign-Reversal Distance Checks
sections.summary: Differential kinematics links position x(t), velocity v(t), and acceleration a(t) for arbitrary non-uniform motion without needing constant-acceleration formulas. Always inspect whether v(t) changes sign inside an interval before equating distance travelled to displacement magnitude.
keyPoints: Fundamental differential links: v = dx/dt; a = dv/dt = d^2x/dt^2 = v (dv/dx). Use a = v dv/dx whenever acceleration is given as a(x) or v(x) rather than a(t).
Distance vs |Displacement|: Displacement = integral(v dt) over [t1, t2]; Distance = integral(|v| dt). Find roots where v(t) = 0 inside (t1, t2), split the integral there, and sum absolute segments.

Average velocity vs average speed: v_avg = Delta r / Delta t (vector), whereas speed_avg = Total Distance / Delta t. For equal time halves: v_avg = (v1 + v2)/2; for equal distance halves: v_avg = 2 v1 v2 / (v1 + v2) (harmonic mean).
Uniformly accelerated equations (vector form for constant a): v = u + at; s = ut + (1/2)at^2; v^2 = u^2 + 2 a . s; s_avg = [(u + v)/2] t; nth second displacement s_n = u + (a/2)(2n - 1).

Galileo's odd-number law & stopping distance: Starting from rest under constant acceleration, displacements in consecutive equal intervals T follow 1 : 3 : 5 : 7... Stopping distance d_stop = u^2 / (2a) scales as u^2; add reaction distance u * t_react if reaction time exists.

Vertical motion under gravity (no drag): Time up = time down = u/g; symmetric heights have equal speeds; total time of flight from tower height H (thrown up at u) obeys -H = u t - (1/2) g t^2, giving t_up * t_down = 2H/g if dropped vs thrown up/down.

sections.heading: Motion Graphs (x-t, v-t, a-t, a-x, v^2-x) & Non-Standard Conversions
sections.summary: Graphical kinematics translates calculus operations into geometric slopes and signed areas across coordinate pairs. Examiners test non-standard axes such as a-x, v-x, and 1/v-x curves where areas and slopes carry disguised physical meanings.
keyPoints: x-t graph: Slope = instantaneous velocity; chord slope = average velocity; concavity (d^2x/dt^2) tells acceleration sign (concave up = a > 0, concave down = a < 0). Sharp corner = infinite acceleration (unphysical impulse).
v-t graph: Slope = acceleration; signed algebraic area = displacement; sum of unsigned |area| above and below t-axis = distance travelled.
a-t graph: Slope = jerk da/dt; area under a-t between t1 and t2 = CHANGE in velocity (v2 - v1), NOT velocity itself (must add initial v1!).
a-x graph: Since a = v dv/dx, area under a-x curve from x1 to x2 equals integral(v dv) = (v2^2 - v1^2) / 2 = Delta(KE) / m.
v^2 vs x graph: Under constant acceleration v^2 = u^2 + 2ax, plot is a straight line with slope = 2a (NOT a!) and y-intercept = u^2.
v vs x graph: Acceleration at any point is a = v * (slope of v-x curve). If v-x is straight line v = v_0 - k x, acceleration is a = -k(v_0 - k x), which is exponentially decaying motion.

sections.heading: 2D Projectile Motion on Horizontal Ground & Elevated Towers
sections.summary: Projectile motion decomposes into independent horizontal uniform motion (a_x = 0) and vertical free fall (a_y = -g) coupled solely by shared flight time t. Expressing trajectory as y(x) = x tan(theta)(1 - x/R) eliminates time completely.
keyPoints: Standard ground-to-ground projection (speed u, angle theta above horizontal): T = 2 u sin(theta) / g; H = u^2 sin^2(theta) / (2g); R = u^2 sin(2 theta) / g. Identity: R / H = 4 cot(theta) => R = 4H at 45 deg.
Complementary launch angles theta and (90 deg - theta) with equal speed u yield IDENTICAL horizontal range R, while T1 / T2 = tan(theta), H1 / H2 = tan^2(theta), and R = 4 sqrt(H1 H2).

Instantaneous kinematics & curvature: At time t, v_x = u cos(theta), v_y = u sin(theta) - gt. At highest point, speed = u cos(theta) != 0, KE = K_0 cos^2(theta), and radius of curvature R_c = v^2 / g_perp = u^2 cos^2(theta) / g (minimum R_c of entire flight!).
Vector velocity angle relation: If velocity becomes perpendicular to initial velocity u after time t (possible only if theta > 45 deg for ground landing), u . v = 0 gives t = u / (g sin theta).

Angular momentum during projectile flight: About point of projection O, gravity exerts non-zero torque tau = -m g x k, so L_O varies continuously, peaking at apex (x = R/2, y = H) with magnitude m (u cos theta) H.

Projection from tower height H (at angle theta above/below horizontal): Resolve along y with y = -H at landing, or use conservation of energy for landing speed v = sqrt(u^2 + 2gH) independent of launch angle!

sections.heading: Projectile Motion on Inclined Planes & Parabolic Safety Envelopes
sections.summary: Tilting the coordinate frame parallel and perpendicular to an incline of angle beta decouples flight time T (from perpendicular zero displacement) from range along the incline. Optimizing launch angle alpha relative to the horizontal yields the maximum up-incline and down-incline ranges.
keyPoints: Coordinate axes along incline (x') and normal to incline (y'): Acceleration components are a_x' = -g sin(beta) (up-incline) or +g sin(beta) (down-incline), and a_y' = -g cos(beta) in both cases.

Upward projection along incline (launch angle theta_0 measured FROM incline, i.e., alpha - beta): Time of flight T = 2 u sin(theta_0) / (g cos beta). Velocity hits incline perpendicularly when v_x' = 0 at t = T => cot(beta) = 2 tan(theta_0).

Maximum range up an incline of angle beta: R_max(up) = u^2 / [g (1 + sin beta)], achieved when launch bisects the angle between incline and vertical: theta_0 = pi/4 - beta/2 (or alpha = pi/4 + beta/2 from horizontal).
Maximum range down an incline of angle beta: R_max(down) = u^2 / [g (1 - sin beta)], achieved at theta_0 = pi/4 + beta/2 (measured above the downward incline).

Elastic rebound on an incline: When a ball dropped from height h hits a smooth incline of angle beta elastically (e = 1), it rebounds horizontally (if beta = 45 deg) or at 2 beta to vertical; first bounce distance along incline is 8 h sin(beta)!

Parabolic safety envelope (locus of farthest reachable points in any direction): y = u^2/(2g) - (g x^2)/(2 u^2). Setting y = 0 recovers max horizontal range u^2/g, and x = 0 recovers max height u^2/(2g).

sections.heading: Relative Velocity: River-Boat, Rain-Umbrella & Closest Approach
sections.summary: Relative velocity v_AB = v_A - v_B transforms multi-body 2D motion into a single-body straight-line problem in the reference frame of B. Dropping a geometric perpendicular from stationary B onto the relative path of A yields exact minimum separation and collision conditions.
keyPoints: Fundamental frame law: v_AB = v_A - v_B and a_AB = a_A - a_B. Two projectiles launched simultaneously in uniform gravity have ZERO relative acceleration (a_rel = 0), so one appears to move in a STRAIGHT LINE relative to the other!

River-boat crossing (river width d, stream v_r, boat speed in still water v_b): Drift x = (v_r - v_b sin theta) * t, crossing time t = d / (v_b cos theta), where theta is steering angle upstream from normal.
Minimum time to cross river: Steer strictly perpendicular to bank (theta = 0) -> t_min = d / v_b (independent of v_r!), with downstream drift x = v_r * (d / v_b).
Shortest path / zero drift crossing: Possible ONLY if v_b > v_r. Steer upstream at sin(theta) = v_r / v_b -> resultant perpendicular speed = sqrt(v_b^2 - v_r^2), time t = d / sqrt(v_b^2 - v_r^2).

Minimum drift when boat is slower than river (v_b < v_r): Zero drift is IMPOSSIBLE. Minimize x = (v_r - v_b sin theta) d / (v_b cos theta) by dx/d(theta) = 0 -> sin(theta) = v_b / v_r (reciprocal of fast-boat condition!), giving x_min = d sqrt(v_r^2 - v_b^2) / v_b.

Rain-umbrella & closest approach: Hold umbrella opposite to v_rain,man = v_rain - v_man. For two particles with initial relative position r_0 and relative velocity v_rel, collision occurs iff r_0 is anti-parallel to v_rel; otherwise d_min = |r_0 x v_rel| / |v_rel| at t_min = -(r_0 . v_rel) / |v_rel|^2.

derivationsAndGraphs.title: Non-Uniform v-t Graph: Displacement vs Distance & a-x Area
derivationsAndGraphs.expressionOrCurve: x2 - x1 = integral(v dt) ; Distance = integral(|v| dt) ; (v2^2 - v1^2)/2 = integral(a dx)
derivationsAndGraphs.keyTakeaway: Whenever v(t) crosses the time axis inside [t1, t2], area below t-axis subtracts from displacement but ADDS to total distance travelled.

derivationsAndGraphs.title: Parabolic Trajectory & Complementary Range Symmetry
derivationsAndGraphs.expressionOrCurve: y = x tan(theta) - g x^2 / (2 u^2 cos^2 theta) = x tan(theta) * (1 - x/R)
derivationsAndGraphs.keyTakeaway: Writing y = x tan(theta)(1 - x/R) solves most missing-angle or clearance-over-wall problems without ever computing time t.

derivationsAndGraphs.title: Up-Incline Maximum Range Optimization
derivationsAndGraphs.expressionOrCurve: R(theta_0) = [2 u^2 sin(theta_0) cos(theta_0 + beta)] / (g cos^2 beta)  =>  R_max = u^2 / [g (1 + sin beta)]
derivationsAndGraphs.keyTakeaway: Using 2 sin A cos B = sin(A+B) + sin(A-B) gives sin(2 theta_0 + beta) + sin(-beta), maximized when 2 theta_0 + beta = 90 deg.

derivationsAndGraphs.title: Minimum Drift Steering Vector Geometry (v_b < v_r)
derivationsAndGraphs.expressionOrCurve: v_resultant perpendicular to v_b  =>  sin(theta_upstream) = v_b / v_r  =>  x_min = (d / v_b) sqrt(v_r^2 - v_b^2)
derivationsAndGraphs.keyTakeaway: Geometrically, tipping the v_b circle tangent to the resultant vector minimizes the drift angle from normal: fast boat uses sin(theta) = v_r/v_b, slow boat uses sin(theta) = v_b/v_r.

formulas.formula: a = dv/dt = v (dv/dx) = (1/2) d(v^2)/dx
formulas.note: Essential when a is given as f(x) or v as f(x)

formulas.formula: v_avg = 2 v1 v2 / (v1 + v2)  [or n / Sum(1/v_i)]
formulas.note: Valid ONLY for equal distance segments; equal times use arithmetic mean
Check if velocity reverses within the n-th second!

formulas.formula: T = 2u sin(theta)/g ; H = u^2 sin^2(theta)/(2g) ; R = u^2 sin(2 theta)/g
formulas.note: R / H = 4 cot(theta); R = 4 sqrt(H1 H2) for complementary angles

formulas.formula: R_c = v^2 / (g cos alpha) = u^2 cos^2(theta) / (g cos^3 alpha)
formulas.note: alpha = instantaneous angle of velocity with horizontal; min at apex

formulas.formula: t = u / (g sin theta)  [exists only if theta > 45 deg for flat ground]
formulas.note: Derived from u . (u + g t) = 0

formulas.formula: T = 2u sin(theta_0)/(g cos beta) ; R_max(up/dn) = u^2 / [g (1 +/- sin beta)]
formulas.note: theta_0 is launch angle measured relative to the incline surface

formulas.formula: tan(theta_0) = cot(beta) / 2  [for perpendicular strike: v_x' = 0]
formulas.note: Equate time to max incline distance to flight time T

formulas.concept: River Crossing Minimum Time & Zero Drift
formulas.formula: t_min = d / v_b ; t_zero_drift = d / sqrt(v_b^2 - v_r^2) (v_b > v_r)
formulas.note: Zero drift steering sin(theta) = v_r / v_b upstream

formulas.concept: Minimum Drift for Slow Boat (v_b < v_r)
formulas.formula: sin(theta) = v_b / v_r ; x_min = d sqrt(v_r^2 - v_b^2) / v_b
formulas.note: Notice v_b/v_r instead of v_r/v_b!

formulas.formula: d_min = |r_0 x v_rel| / |v_rel| ; t_min = -(r_0 . v_rel) / |v_rel|^2
formulas.note: If t_min < 0, particles are already separating and d_min = |r_0|

traps: Distance != |Displacement| when velocity flips sign! In s_n = u + (a/2)(2n-1) with u = +15 m/s and a = -10 m/s^2, s_2 = 0 displacement, yet actual distance in the 2nd second (t=1 to 2, stopping at t=1.5) is 2 x 1.25 = 2.5 m!
At highest point of a projectile, velocity is u cos(theta) horizontally (NOT zero), acceleration is g downward (NOT zero), and speed is minimum.
Angle measured from VERTICAL trap: If launch angle phi is given from vertical instead of horizontal, H = u^2 cos^2(phi)/(2g) — do NOT blindly plug phi into sin^2!
In a-t graphs, students frequently equate area under a-t directly to final velocity v, forgetting to add initial velocity u!
In v^2 vs x linear graphs, slope is 2a (NOT a!). Halving the slope gives the true acceleration.
Two-projectile collision in mid-air: Since a_rel = g - g = 0, relative motion is purely straight-line; collision occurs if and only if v_rel points along r_2 - r_1!
revisionChecklist: Derive distance vs displacement in the exact second where a decelerating particle momentarily stops and reverses.
Verify slopes and area meanings of x-t, v-t, a-t, a-x, and v^2-x graphs.
Recall trajectory equation y = x tan(theta)(1 - x/R) and minimum radius of curvature at apex.
Derive maximum range up and down an inclined plane of angle beta.
Verify both steering angles sin(theta) = v_r/v_b (fast boat zero drift) and sin(theta) = v_b/v_r (slow boat min drift).
Recall closest approach formula d_min = |r_0 x v_rel| / |v_rel| and check t_min > 0.
Check R / H = 4 cot(theta) and R = 4 sqrt(H1 H2) for complementary launches.

solvedExamples.question: A particle is projected vertically upward with u = 25 m/s (g = 10 m/s^2). Find the distance travelled and displacement during the 3rd second of motion (from t = 2 s to t = 3 s).
steps: Check turning point (v = 0): 0 = 25 - 10 t => t = 2.5 s, which lies strictly inside [2 s, 3 s].
Compute net displacement via s_3 = u + (a/2)(2*3 - 1) = 25 - 5(5) = 0 m.
Find upward distance from t = 2 s to t = 2.5 s: v(2) = 25 - 20 = 5 m/s; d_up = (5)(0.5) - 0.5(10)(0.25) = 1.25 m.
Find downward distance from t = 2.5 s to t = 3 s: d_down = 0.5(10)(0.5)^2 = 1.25 m.
Total distance travelled in 3rd second = 1.25 + 1.25 = 2.5 m.
solvedExamples.pitfall: Reporting 0 m as the distance by blindly applying s_n = u + a(2n-1)/2.

solvedExamples.question: A boat moves with speed 3 km/h in still water across a 1 km wide river flowing at 5 km/h. Find the minimum possible downstream drift and the steering angle upstream from normal.
steps: Here v_b = 3 < v_r = 5, so zero drift is impossible.
For minimum drift when v_b < v_r, steer upstream such that sin(theta) = v_b / v_r = 3 / 5 = 0.6.
Hence steering angle from normal = arcsin(3/5) = 37 degrees upstream (127 deg from downstream flow).
Compute minimum drift: x_min = (d / v_b) * sqrt(v_r^2 - v_b^2) = (1 / 3) * sqrt(25 - 9) = 4/3 km = 1.33 km.
solvedExamples.answer: Drift_min = 4/3 km at 37 deg upstream from normal
solvedExamples.pitfall: Using sin(theta) = v_r/v_b = 5/3 > 1 and concluding no angle exists, or steering straight across (which gives 5/3 km > 4/3 km drift!).

solvedExamples.question: A body starts from rest at x = 0 and moves along +x with acceleration a(x) = (4 - 0.5 x) m/s^2. Find its speed at x = 8 m and maximum speed attained.
steps: Use a = v (dv/dx) => integral(v dv) = integral((4 - 0.5 x) dx).
Speed is maximum where dv/dx = 0 => a = 0 => 4 - 0.5 x = 0 => x = 8 m; thus at x = 8 m, v_max = 4 sqrt(2) m/s.
solvedExamples.answer: v = 4 sqrt(2) m/s (which is also v_max)
solvedExamples.pitfall: Integrating a with respect to t instead of x; a(x) MUST be integrated via v dv = a dx.

solvedExamples.question: A projectile is launched from the foot of an incline of angle 30 deg at speed u = 20 m/s such that it strikes the incline perpendicularly. Find the launch angle theta_0 relative to the incline and the distance along the incline (g = 10 m/s^2).
steps: Time of flight on incline: T = 2 u sin(theta_0) / (g cos beta).
For perpendicular strike, parallel velocity v_x' vanishes at t = T: u cos(theta_0) - g sin(beta) * T = 0.
Substitute T: u cos(theta_0) = g sin(beta) * [2 u sin(theta_0) / (g cos beta)] => cot(theta_0) = 2 tan(beta) => tan(theta_0) = cot(30 deg)/2 = sqrt(3)/2.
Find cos(theta_0) = 2/sqrt(7), sin(theta_0) = sqrt(3)/sqrt(7); T = 2(20)(sqrt(3)/sqrt(7)) / (10 * sqrt(3)/2) = 8/sqrt(7) s.
Distance along incline R = u cos(theta_0) T - (1/2) g sin(beta) T^2 = (1/2) u cos(theta_0) T = 0.5 * 20 * (2/sqrt(7)) * (8/sqrt(7)) = 160/7 m ~ 22.86 m.
solvedExamples.pitfall: Assuming perpendicular strike occurs at maximum up-incline range; optimal angle for R_max is 45 - beta/2 = 30 deg, whereas perpendicular strike has tan(theta_0) = sqrt(3)/2 (~40.9 deg).

weightageNote: Weightage: 4-6% (1-2 questions across pulley constraints, friction stacks, pseudo-force wedges & banked circular turns).
syllabusAlert: Syllabus Sync: Complete Newton's Laws, Impulse-Momentum, Constraints, Pseudo Force, Static/Kinetic Friction & Circular Dynamics are retained across JEE Mains, NEET UG, and JEE Advanced.

sections.heading: Newton's Laws, Free Body Diagrams & Spring-Cut / String-Cut Transients
sections.summary: An isolated Free Body Diagram (FBD) includes every real contact and field force acting ON the body (never forces exerted BY the body). Ideal inextensible strings adjust tension discontinuously upon cutting, whereas ideal springs preserve their instantaneous force kx continuously at t = 0+.
keyPoints: Newton's Second Law in full generality: F_ext = dp/dt = m(dv/dt) + v(dm/dt). For constant mass, F_net = m a along each orthogonal axis independently.

Impulse-Momentum Theorem: Impulse J = integral(F dt) = p_final - p_initial = area under F-t graph. Impulsive forces (normal/tension during collision or sudden tautening of slack string) dominate finite forces like mg over dt -> 0.
Lami's Theorem (3 concurrent coplanar forces in equilibrium): F1 / sin(alpha) = F2 / sin(beta) = F3 / sin(gamma), where alpha is angle opposite F1.

Spring-cut vs String-cut at t = 0+: Cutting a spring drops its force kx to 0 instantaneously. Cutting a string drops that string's tension to 0 instantaneously while any attached spring retains kx = F_old at t = 0+, producing a jump in acceleration!
Inextensible taut string tension: Same throughout a single massless frictionless pulley-string segment. With pulley inertia I or friction, T1 != T2 and T1 - T2 = I alpha / R.
Elevator apparent weight: Normal reaction N = m(g + a_up) = m(g - a_down). During free fall (a_down = g), N = 0 (weightlessness).

sections.heading: Constraint Relations, Movable Pulleys & Wedge-Block Systems
sections.summary: Kinematics of interconnected pulleys and sliding wedges obeys inextensible string-length invariance and normal-surface contact continuity. Virtual work theorem Sum(T . v) = 0 solves multi-pulley acceleration constraints in one algebraic line.
keyPoints: Virtual work constraint: For massless inextensible strings, net power delivered by tension across the whole system vanishes: Sum(T_i . v_i) = 0 and Sum(T_i . a_i) = 0 (take + if T and a align, - if opposite).
Movable pulley kinematics: If pulley moves with velocity v_p and two vertical rope ends move at v1, v2 (same sign convention), then v_p = (v1 + v2)/2 and a_p = (a1 + a2)/2.

Wedge-block normal constraint: When block slides on a moving wedge (incline angle theta) maintaining contact, their velocity/acceleration components perpendicular to the contact interface MUST match: a_block_perp = a_wedge * sin(theta).
Atwood machine with unequal masses (m1 > m2): a = (m1 - m2) g / (m1 + m2); T = 2 m1 m2 g / (m1 + m2); load on ceiling pulley clamp = 2 T = 4 m1 m2 g / (m1 + m2) < (m1 + m2)g always (since AM > HM!).
Inclined Atwood / Double incline (angles alpha, beta): Compare m1 g sin(alpha) vs m2 g sin(beta) to pick acceleration direction, then a = (m1 sin alpha - m2 sin beta)g / (m1 + m2).

sections.heading: Pseudo Force & Non-Inertial Reference Frames
sections.summary: Applying Newton's laws inside a frame accelerating at a_frame requires adding a fictitious pseudo force F_p = -m a_frame to every particle of mass m. This converts dynamic wedge and accelerated-vehicle problems into static equilibrium.
keyPoints: Pseudo force rule: Magnitude = m |a_frame|, direction = strictly OPPOSITE to frame acceleration a_frame (does NOT depend on particle's own acceleration!).
Effective gravity vector g_eff = g - a_frame: In an accelerating car (a forward), plumb bob tilts backward at tan(theta) = a / g with tension T = m sqrt(g^2 + a^2).
Smooth wedge equilibrium: To keep block of mass m stationary on a smooth wedge of angle theta, push wedge horizontally with a = g tan(theta); normal reaction N = m g / cos(theta) (NOT mg cos theta!).

Minimum/maximum wedge acceleration with rough incline (mu, theta): With friction, block stays stationary relative to wedge for a_min = g (sin theta - mu cos theta)/(cos theta + mu sin theta) <= a <= g (sin theta + mu cos theta)/(cos theta - mu sin theta).
Newton's 3rd Law check: Pseudo forces have NO action-reaction pair because they do not arise from real physical interactions.

sections.heading: Static vs Kinetic Friction, Angle of Repose & Two-Block Stacks
sections.summary: Static friction is self-adjusting up to a limiting threshold mu_s N to oppose impending relative slip, whereas kinetic friction assumes a constant value mu_k N opposing actual relative velocity. Two-block friction problems test whether internal friction suffices to accelerate the passive block together with the driven block.
keyPoints: Static vs Kinetic regime: 0 <= f_s <= f_s,max = mu_s N; once slip starts, f_k = mu_k N (typically mu_k <= mu_s). Friction ALWAYS opposes RELATIVE motion/tendency between contacting surfaces, NOT necessarily absolute motion!

Angle of friction (lambda) & Angle of Repose (theta_r): tan(lambda) = mu_s (angle between resultant contact force R = sqrt(N^2 + f^2) and N). Block on rough ramp begins sliding when ramp angle theta >= theta_r = arctan(mu_s).

Optimal pulling/pushing angle on rough flat floor: Minimum pulling force F_min = mu m g / sqrt(1 + mu^2) = m g sin(lambda), applied UPWARD at angle lambda = arctan(mu) to horizontal. Pushing at angle phi downward requires F = mu mg / (cos phi - mu sin phi), impossible if tan phi >= 1/mu!

Two-block stack algorithm (top m, bottom M, friction mu1 between blocks, smooth floor): (1) Assume no slip -> common a_c = F / (m + M); (2) Find required friction on passive block: f_req = m * a_c (if F pulls M) or M * a_c (if F pulls m); (3) Compare f_req <= f_max = mu1 m g; if exceeded, blocks slip with kinetic friction f_max accelerating the passive block.
Rough incline block-push range: To hold block m stationary on ramp (theta > theta_r), F_min = mg(sin theta - mu cos theta) up-ramp, and F_max = mg(sin theta + mu cos theta) before pushing it upward.

sections.heading: Circular Dynamics: Flat/Banked Tracks, Conical Pendulum & Death Well
sections.summary: Circular motion requires a net radial inward centripetal force m v^2 / r = m omega^2 r perpendicular to instantaneous velocity. Tangential acceleration a_t = dv/dt alters speed while centripetal acceleration a_c = v^2 / r turns the velocity vector.
keyPoints: Total acceleration in non-uniform circular motion: a_net = sqrt(a_c^2 + a_t^2) = sqrt((v^2/r)^2 + (dv/dt)^2). Centripetal force is NOT a separate force — it is the net radial inward component of real forces (N, T, f, mg).

Flat rough turn (radius r, mu): Friction provides centripetal force -> v_max = sqrt(mu g r). Overturning limit on flat road occurs BEFORE skidding if track width/2h < mu (v_overturn = sqrt(g r d / (2h))).
Ideal frictionless banked road (angle theta): N sin theta = m v^2 / r and N cos theta = m g -> optimum speed v_0 = sqrt(r g tan theta) requires ZERO lateral friction.

Rough banked road speed window: Above v_0, car tends to skid UPWARD so friction points DOWN the slope: v_max = sqrt( r g (sin theta + mu cos theta) / (cos theta - mu sin theta) ). Below v_0, friction points UP slope: v_min = sqrt( r g (sin theta - mu cos theta) / (cos theta + mu sin theta) ) (if tan theta > mu).

Conical pendulum (string L, angle theta with vertical): T cos theta = mg, T sin theta = m omega^2 (L sin theta) -> omega = sqrt(g / (L cos theta)), Period T_p = 2 pi sqrt((L cos theta) / g). Notice vertical height h = L cos theta controls period!
Rotor / Death well (vertical cylinder radius R, mu): N = m omega^2 R, friction balances weight f = mg <= mu N -> minimum angular speed omega_min = sqrt(g / (mu R)).

derivationsAndGraphs.title: Friction vs Applied Force Graph (Static Peak to Kinetic Plateau)
derivationsAndGraphs.expressionOrCurve: f = F_applied (45 deg line up to F = mu_s N), slight drop to constant horizontal line f_k = mu_k N
derivationsAndGraphs.keyTakeaway: Static friction exactly equals driving force until F exceeds mu_s N; never plug mu_s N blindly when the block is stationary under a smaller load.

derivationsAndGraphs.title: Virtual Work Pulley Constraint Proof
derivationsAndGraphs.expressionOrCurve: Sum(L_i) = const => Sum(dL_i/dt) = 0 => Sum(T_i . v_i) = 0 => Sum(T_i . a_i) = 0
derivationsAndGraphs.keyTakeaway: Eliminates manual string-segment algebra in multi-pulley blocks: count strands pulling each block and equate Sum(n_i T a_i) = 0.

derivationsAndGraphs.title: Two-Block Acceleration vs Applied Force Graph
derivationsAndGraphs.expressionOrCurve: a1 = a2 = F/(m+M) for F <= F_crit ; beyond F_crit, passive block saturates at a_max = f_max / m_passive while driven block slope steepens
derivationsAndGraphs.keyTakeaway: Before slip, both lines share slope 1/(m+M); after slip, passive block line becomes horizontal and driven block slope jumps to 1/m_driven.

derivationsAndGraphs.title: Rough Banked Track Minimum & Maximum Speed Bounds
derivationsAndGraphs.expressionOrCurve: v^2 / (r g) = (tan theta +/- mu) / (1 -/+ mu tan theta) = tan(theta +/- lambda)
derivationsAndGraphs.keyTakeaway: Writing v_max = sqrt(r g tan(theta + lambda)) and v_min = sqrt(r g tan(theta - lambda)) where mu = tan(lambda) makes memorization effortless!

comparison.title: Spring-Cut vs String-Cut & Circular Track Regimes
rows: Any taut string attached adjusts T instantaneously
Spring keeps kx = F_old at t = 0+
Do NOT assume spring relaxes instantaneously!
At equilibrium on flat ground with F=0, f_s = 0 (not mu_s N!)
Can accelerate a passive upper block forward!
v_min = sqrt(rg tan(theta - lambda)) if theta > lambda

traps: Blindly setting static friction f = mu_s N: When a 5 kg block (mu_s = 0.5, f_max = 25 N) is pushed with 10 N, actual friction is 10 N, NOT 25 N!
Pushing angle trap: Pushing a block downward at angle phi > (90 - lambda) (i.e. tan phi >= 1/mu) CANNOT move the block no matter how huge the force F is (self-locking)!
Pseudo force direction error: F_p points strictly opposite to frame acceleration a_frame — NEVER opposite to the block's velocity or relative motion.
Spring-cut vs String-cut: When a string supporting a lower hanging mass via a spring is cut, the upper block's spring tension stays intact at t = 0+, doubling or reversing its acceleration!
Normal reaction on wedge with horizontal acceleration a_wedge = g tan(theta): N = mg / cos(theta), NOT mg cos(theta)! (Because N cos(theta) = mg).
Centripetal force is NOT a separate force on an FBD! Drawing 'mv^2/r outward' AND working in the inertial ground frame double-counts the force and flips signs.
revisionChecklist: Verify Sum(T . a) = 0 sign rules on a 3-pulley system.
Contrast instantaneous t = 0+ accelerations when cutting a string vs cutting a spring.
Derive smooth wedge acceleration a = g tan(theta) and N = mg / cos(theta) using both ground and wedge frames.
Practice both two-block stack cases: F applied on lower block M vs F applied on upper block m (with and without floor friction).
Recall minimum pulling force F_min = mg sin(lambda) at optimal angle lambda = arctan(mu).
Derive v_max and v_min on a rough banked track in terms of tan(theta +/- lambda).
Recall conical pendulum T = 2 pi sqrt(L cos theta / g) and death well omega_min = sqrt(g / mu R).

solvedExamples.question: Two blocks m1 = 2 kg (upper) and m2 = 3 kg (lower) hang from a ceiling via a massless string (above m1) and an ideal spring (between m1 and m2). The system is in static equilibrium. If the top string is suddenly cut, find the instantaneous accelerations of m1 and m2 just after the cut (g = 10 m/s^2).
steps: Before cut (equilibrium): Spring supports m2 => F_spring = m2 g = 3 x 10 = 30 N; Top string supports both => T = (m1 + m2) g = 50 N.
Just after top string is cut (t = 0+): Top tension drops immediately to T = 0, while spring extension cannot change instantaneously so F_spring stays 30 N.
FBD of m2 at t = 0+: Downward m2 g = 30 N, upward F_spring = 30 N => a2 = (30 - 30)/3 = 0 m/s^2.
FBD of m1 at t = 0+: Downward m1 g = 20 N PLUS downward spring pull F_spring = 30 N => F_net = 50 N downward.
Acceleration of m1: a1 = 50 / 2 = 25 m/s^2 downward.
solvedExamples.pitfall: Writing a1 = a2 = g = 10 m/s^2 by assuming the spring force vanishes immediately.

solvedExamples.question: A 2 kg block rests on a rough 37 deg incline (mu_s = 0.5, g = 10 m/s^2). Find the minimum and maximum horizontal force F required to keep the block stationary on the incline (sin 37 = 3/5, cos 37 = 4/5).
steps: Resolve forces along and perpendicular to incline: N = mg cos 37 + F sin 37 = 16 + 0.6 F.
Gravity component down incline = mg sin 37 = 12 N; horizontal F component up incline = F cos 37 = 0.8 F.
For F_min (block about to slide DOWN, friction UP incline): 0.8 F_min + 0.5(16 + 0.6 F_min) = 12 => 1.1 F_min + 8 = 12 => F_min = 4 / 1.1 = 40/11 N.
For F_max (block about to slide UP, friction DOWN incline): 0.8 F_max = 12 + 0.5(16 + 0.6 F_max) => 0.5 F_max = 20 => F_max = 40 N.
solvedExamples.pitfall: Forgetting the F sin 37 contribution to Normal reaction N!

solvedExamples.question: A car negotiates a flat circular bend of radius 40 m on a road with coefficient of static friction mu = 0.4. What is the maximum safe speed without skidding (g = 10 m/s^2)?
steps: Centripetal force is supplied entirely by static friction: m v^2 / r <= f_max = mu m g.
Mass m cancels from both sides: v^2 <= mu g r.
Substitute values: v_max = sqrt(0.4 x 10 x 40) = sqrt(160) = 4 sqrt(10) m/s.
Numerical estimate: 4 x 3.162 = 12.65 m/s (~ 45.5 km/h).
solvedExamples.pitfall: Confusing radius with diameter or using kinetic friction instead of static friction (tires roll without lateral slip until skid threshold).

solvedExamples.question: A wedge of mass M = 4 kg (smooth incline theta = 37 deg) rests on a rough horizontal floor (mu = 0.5). A block of mass m = 2 kg is placed on the wedge and released. Check whether the wedge slips on the floor, and find the floor friction force if it stays stationary (g = 10 m/s^2).
steps: Assume wedge remains at rest: Block accelerates down smooth incline at a = g sin 37 = 6 m/s^2, and normal reaction N1 = m g cos 37 = 2 x 10 x 0.8 = 16 N.
On the wedge, N1 acts perpendicular to incline (downward and backward horizontally): Horizontal push N1 sin 37 = 16 x 0.6 = 9.6 N; Vertical push N1 cos 37 = 16 x 0.8 = 12.8 N.
Normal reaction from floor on wedge: N_floor = M g + N1 cos 37 = 40 + 12.8 = 52.8 N.
Maximum static friction available from floor: f_max = mu N_floor = 0.5 x 52.8 = 26.4 N.
Since required horizontal balancing friction 9.6 N < 26.4 N, the wedge stays stationary and floor static friction equals 9.6 N.
solvedExamples.answer: Wedge does NOT slip; static friction = 9.6 N
solvedExamples.pitfall: Setting N_floor = (M + m)g = 60 N! Because the block accelerates downward at a_y = g sin^2(theta), N_floor is strictly LESS than (M + m)g.

weightageNote: Weightage: 5-7% (2 questions in JEE Mains & NEET UG; foundational energy/momentum bridge in JEE Advanced).
syllabusAlert: Syllabus Sync: Work-Energy Theorem, Conservative Forces, Potential Wells, Vertical Circular Motion, Centre of Mass (including cavities), Momentum Conservation & 1D/2D Collisions (e) are 100% retained.

sections.heading: Work Done by Constant, Variable & Frame-Dependent Forces
sections.summary: Mechanical work dW = F . dr quantifies energy transferred to a particle along its actual path. Because displacement dr depends on the observer's reference frame, work done by individual forces (like static friction or normal reaction) is frame-dependent.
keyPoints: Line integral definition: W = integral(F . dr) = integral(F_x dx + F_y dy + F_z dz). Graphically, signed area under F_x vs x equals work done.
Spring force work: W_spring = -(1/2) k (x_f^2 - x_i^2) depends ONLY on initial and final deformations from natural length (conservative!). Never forget the x_i^2 term when already stretched!

Work by static friction: Can be POSITIVE (e.g., upper block accelerated by moving lower truck in ground frame), NEGATIVE, or ZERO, though the net work across BOTH contacting surfaces together is ALWAYS zero (no relative slip!).
Work by kinetic friction: Across a pair of sliding surfaces, total work by kinetic friction is ALWAYS strictly negative: W_k,net = -f_k * d_relative < 0 (converted to thermal heat).

Pulling hanging chain onto smooth table: If length l (mass m_l = M l / L) hangs vertically over edge, its COM sits at depth l/2 below table, so minimum work to pull it up is W = m_l g (l/2) = M g l^2 / (2L).

sections.heading: Work-Energy Theorem, Mechanical Power & Constant-Power Motion
sections.summary: The Work-Energy Theorem W_all = K_f - K_i holds unconditionally across both inertial and non-inertial frames (provided pseudo-force work is included). Instantaneous power P = F . v governs vehicle acceleration ceilings and variable-speed kinematics.
keyPoints: Work-Energy Theorem (WET): W_c + W_nc + W_ext + W_pseudo = Delta K. Use WET whenever a question mixes curved paths, variable forces, or friction without asking for intermediate times.
Conservation of Mechanical Energy: E = K + U stays constant ONLY when W_nc = 0 and W_ext = 0 (or when non-conservative/constraint forces like normal reaction do zero work).
Instantaneous & Average Power: P_inst = dW/dt = F . v = F v cos(theta); P_avg = Delta W / Delta t = Delta K / Delta t.

Constant-Power Kinematics (P = const from rest): P = m v (dv/dt) => v^2 = 2 P t / m => v proportional to t^(1/2); integrating gives x = sqrt(8 P / 9m) * t^(3/2) proportional to t^(3/2), and a proportional to t^(-1/2)!
Pump power lifting water: Lifting mass rate (dm/dt) to height h and ejecting at speed v requires minimum power P = (dm/dt)(g h + v^2 / 2).

sections.heading: Conservative Forces, Potential Energy Wells & Equilibrium Stability
sections.summary: A force is conservative if curl F = 0 (work around every closed loop vanishes), allowing definition of a scalar potential U(r) with F = -grad U. Analyzing U(x) curves reveals equilibrium positions, stability, oscillation frequency, and forbidden regions.
keyPoints: Exact derivative relation: In 1D, F_x = -dU/dx (negative slope of U-x curve); in 3D, F = -(dU/dx i + dU/dy j + dU/dz k). Check curl F = 0 (dF_x/dy = dF_y/dx) to verify conservativeness!
Equilibrium condition: F = 0 <=> dU/dx = 0 (stationary points on U-x graph).

Three equilibrium classes: (1) Stable: d^2U/dx^2 > 0 (U is local MINIMUM, slight displacement creates restoring force); (2) Unstable: d^2U/dx^2 < 0 (U is local MAXIMUM); (3) Neutral: d^2U/dx^2 = 0 over an interval.
Small-oscillation SHM near stable minimum x_0: Effective spring constant k_eff = (d^2U/dx^2)|_{x0}, giving angular frequency omega = sqrt(k_eff / m).
Turning points & allowed region: Since K = E - U(x) >= 0, particle is strictly confined to regions where U(x) <= E_total; intersections U(x) = E mark instantaneous rest turning points.

sections.heading: Vertical Circular Motion (Loop-the-Loop, String Slackening & Sphere Slide)
sections.summary: Gravity varies particle speed continuously around a vertical circle, making radial equilibrium T +/- mg cos(theta) = m v^2 / R angle-dependent. Distinguishing string/single-track constraints (T >= 0) from rigid-rod/double-track constraints is essential.
keyPoints: Mass m on string/inside single loop of radius R (angle theta from lowest point): Speed v^2 = u^2 - 2 g R (1 - cos theta); Radial equilibrium T - m g cos(theta) = m v^2 / R yields T = m u^2 / R - 2 m g + 3 m g cos(theta).
Universal tension difference: For ANY looping speed u >= sqrt(5 g R), T_bottom - T_top = 6 m g identically! At horizontal (theta = 90 deg), T_bottom - T_horiz = 3 m g.
Critical loop thresholds (String / Inner Loop): Bottom u_min = sqrt(5 g R) -> horizontal speed sqrt(3 g R), top speed sqrt(g R) where T_top = 0.
Rigid massless rod / Double circular track: Rod can push outward (negative tension allowed), so particle merely needs v_top >= 0 => u_min(bottom) = sqrt(4 g R) = 2 sqrt(g R).

Regime switching (String slackening): If u <= sqrt(2 g R), particle oscillates like a pendulum below horizontal (never exceeds 90 deg). If sqrt(2 g R) < u < sqrt(5 g R), string goes slack (T = 0) at cos theta = (2gR - u^2)/(3gR) above horizontal (90 < theta < 180) and particle switches to parabolic projectile motion!
Sliding off smooth sphere of radius R from top (u = 0): Normal N drops to 0 at vertical drop h = R/3 (angle cos theta = 2/3 from vertical, theta ~ 48.2 deg), speed v = sqrt(2 g R / 3).

sections.heading: Centre of Mass (COM), Cavity Subtraction & Momentum Conservation
sections.summary: The Centre of Mass moves as if total mass M were concentrated there and acted upon solely by external forces (M a_cm = F_ext). Zero net external force keeps COM velocity constant during internal explosions, recoils, and man-plank displacements.
keyPoints: Standard COM positions (measured from base/centre): Uniform semicircular ring y_cm = 2R/pi; Semicircular disc y_cm = 4R/(3pi); Hollow hemisphere y_cm = R/2; Solid hemisphere y_cm = 3R/8; Hollow cone h/3 from base; Solid cone h/4 from base; Triangular plate h/3 from base.

Cavity COM trick (negative mass superposition): x_cm = (M_full x_full - M_cav x_cav) / (M_full - M_cav). Be careful: for 2D uniform plates mass scales with Area; for 3D solids mass scales with Volume!

Zero-external-force COM shift: If initially at rest (v_cm = 0), internal motion enforces Sum(m_i Delta r_i) = 0. For man of mass m walking distance L on plank M (smooth floor): plank shifts opposite by x = m L / (m + M).

Shell explosion in mid-air: Explosion is purely internal, so COM continues along the exact original parabolic trajectory until fragments hit ground! If one fragment falls vertically from apex, solve m1 x1 + m2 x2 = (m1 + m2) R.
Recoil & variable impulse: Conserve linear momentum along directions where Sum(F_ext) = 0 (e.g., horizontal axis on smooth floor even if vertical gravity + normal act!).

sections.heading: 1D & 2D Collisions, Coefficient of Restitution & Bouncing Balls
sections.summary: During impact along the Line of Impact (LOI), normal impulse transfers momentum while perpendicular tangential velocity stays unchanged for smooth bodies. Newton's restitution law e = (v2 - v1)_sep / (u1 - u2)_app bridges elastic (e = 1) and perfectly inelastic (e = 0) impacts.
keyPoints: 1D collision final velocities: v1 = [(m1 - e m2) u1 + (1 + e) m2 u2] / (m1 + m2); v2 = [(m2 - e m1) u2 + (1 + e) m1 u1] / (m1 + m2). Check special cases: if e=1 and m1=m2, velocities swap! If e=1 and m2 >> m1 (wall at rest), light ball bounces at -u1.
Kinetic energy loss in any 1D collision: Delta K_loss = (1/2) * [m1 m2 / (m1 + m2)] * (u1 - u2)^2 * (1 - e^2). Maximum allowed loss occurs at e = 0 (bodies stick together with v_common = v_cm).

2D Oblique collision (smooth spheres): Tangential components perpendicular to LOI (line joining centres at impact) stay UNCHANGED for each sphere; apply momentum conservation and restitution e ONLY along LOI!
Equal-mass 2D elastic collision (m1 = m2, e = 1, target initially at rest): Two spheres ALWAYS separate at 90 degrees (theta_1 + theta_2 = 90 deg) because p1 . p2 = 0 from p_i^2 = p1^2 + p2^2!

Ballistic / Bouncing ball on floor (dropped from H, restitution e): Speed after n-th bounce v_n = e^n sqrt(2gH); rebound height h_n = e^(2n) H; total distance travelled = H (1 + e^2)/(1 - e^2); total time to stop = sqrt(2H/g) * (1 + e)/(1 - e).

derivationsAndGraphs.keyTakeaway: Only the relative kinetic energy (1/2) mu v_rel^2 can be dissipated in a collision; COM kinetic energy (1/2)(m1+m2)v_cm^2 is strictly locked by momentum conservation!

comparison.title: Vertical Circular Motion & Collision Regime Matrix
rows: Switches to projectile parabola at cos(theta) = (2gR - u^2)/(3gR)
Equal masses swap velocities (1D) or split at 90 deg (2D)
Bodies stick together moving at v_cm

traps: Work by static friction is NOT always zero! In ground frame, static friction on a crate accelerating on a truck bed does positive work (+), while friction on the truck does equal negative work (-).
Spring energy trap: Compressing/stretching a spring ALREADY stretched by x1 to x2 requires W = (1/2)k(x2^2 - x1^2), NOT (1/2)k(x2 - x1)^2!
Vertical circle rod vs string: Do NOT give sqrt(5gR) when the mass is mounted on a light rigid rod or sliding inside a narrow double-walled circular tube — both need only sqrt(4gR)!
Cavity COM area vs volume error: For a circular disc with a circular hole, mass is proportional to R^2 (area); for a solid sphere with a spherical hole, mass is proportional to R^3 (volume)!
Bouncing ball e trap: If ball drops from h1 and rebounds to h2, e = sqrt(h2 / h1), NOT h2 / h1!
2D oblique impact: Restitution equation applies ONLY to velocity components ALONG the normal (Line of Impact), NEVER to total speeds!

Derive constant-power relations v ~ t^(1/2), x ~ t^(3/2), and v^3 ~ x.
Analyze a U(x) graph to mark stable, unstable, neutral equilibria and turning points for given E.
Verify critical speeds for vertical circle: string sqrt(5gR) vs rod sqrt(4gR) vs pendulum limit sqrt(2gR).
Recall COM formulas for semi-ring, semi-disc, hollow/solid hemisphere, and hollow/solid cone.
Derive Delta K_loss = (1/2) mu (u1 - u2)^2 (1 - e^2) and prove equal-mass elastic oblique 90 deg separation.
Verify infinite bouncing ball total distance and total time formulas.

solvedExamples.question: A 1000 kg car accelerates from rest under constant engine power P = 40 kW on a flat frictionless road. Find its speed and distance covered after t = 9 seconds.
steps: By Work-Energy Theorem with constant power P: K(t) = P * t => (1/2) m v^2 = P t.
Solve for v: v = sqrt(2 P t / m) = sqrt(2 x 40000 x 9 / 1000) = sqrt(720) = 12 sqrt(5) ~ 26.83 m/s.
Integrate v(t) = sqrt(2 P / m) * t^(1/2) from 0 to t: x = (2/3) sqrt(2 P / m) * t^(3/2).
solvedExamples.answer: v = 12 sqrt(5) m/s ; x = 72 sqrt(5) m
solvedExamples.pitfall: Using x = (1/2) v t = 54 sqrt(5) m assumes constant acceleration, whereas here a decreases as t^(-1/2) so x = (2/3) v t!

solvedExamples.question: From a uniform circular disc of radius R, a circular hole of diameter R is cut out such that the hole's circumference touches the centre and outer rim of the disc. Find the distance of the remaining plate's COM from the disc centre.
steps: Place disc centre at origin (0, 0); let hole centre be at x = +R/2 with radius r = R/2.
Since disc is uniform 2D, mass is proportional to area: M_full ~ pi R^2, M_hole ~ pi (R/2)^2 = M_full / 4.
Apply negative-mass superposition: x_cm = [M_full(0) - (M_full/4)(R/2)] / [M_full - M_full/4].
Simplify: x_cm = -(R/8) / (3/4) = -R / 6 (shifted R/6 opposite to the hole).
solvedExamples.pitfall: Using R^3 (sphere volume ratio 1/8 -> R/14) instead of R^2 (disc area ratio 1/4 -> R/6)!

solvedExamples.question: A particle of mass m slides from rest from the top of a smooth fixed hemisphere of radius R. At what vertical height above the flat base does it lose contact with the hemisphere?
steps: Let particle lose contact (N = 0) at angle theta from vertical; vertical drop from top is h = R(1 - cos theta).
Energy conservation: (1/2) m v^2 = m g R (1 - cos theta) => v^2 = 2 g R (1 - cos theta).
Radial equation at loss of contact (N = 0): m g cos(theta) = m v^2 / R.
Substitute v^2: g cos(theta) = 2 g (1 - cos theta) => 3 cos(theta) = 2 => cos(theta) = 2/3.
Height above base = R cos(theta) = 2 R / 3 (i.e., R/3 below the top).
solvedExamples.pitfall: Reporting drop from top (R/3) when the question asks height above the base (2R/3)!

solvedExamples.question: A 2 kg ball moving at 6 m/s collides head-on with a stationary 4 kg ball with coefficient of restitution e = 1/2. Find the final velocities of both balls and the percentage of initial kinetic energy lost.
steps: Momentum conservation: 2(6) + 0 = 2 v1 + 4 v2 => v1 + 2 v2 = 6.
Restitution along LOI: v2 - v1 = e (u1 - u2) = 0.5 (6 - 0) = 3.
Add equations: 3 v2 = 9 => v2 = +3 m/s, and v1 = 3 - 3 = 0 m/s!
solvedExamples.answer: v1 = 0 m/s, v2 = 3 m/s ; 50% KE lost
solvedExamples.pitfall: Assuming v1 cannot become zero in an inelastic collision; here m2 = 2 m1 and e = 1/2 gives m1 - e m2 = 0, stopping the first ball completely!

weightageNote: Weightage: 6-8% (Highest-yield Mechanics chapter across JEE Mains, NEET UG, and IIT JEE Advanced: MOI, Rolling & Angular Momentum).
syllabusAlert: Syllabus Sync: Rotational kinematics, Moment of Inertia, Parallel & Perpendicular Axes Theorems, Torque, Equilibrium, Toppling, Pure Rolling & Conservation of Angular Momentum are 100% retained.

sections.heading: Moment of Inertia (MOI), Radius of Gyration & Axis Theorems
sections.summary: Moment of inertia I = integral(r^2 dm) quantifies rotational resistance around a specific axis, scaling with mass and squared perpendicular distance. Combining Parallel and Perpendicular Axes Theorems with cavity subtraction derives the MOI of virtually any rigid composite body.
keyPoints: Standard I_cm values (and k^2/R^2 ratios): Thin ring/hollow cylinder about symmetry axis = MR^2 (1); Uniform disc/solid cylinder = MR^2/2 (1/2); Hollow spherical shell = 2/3 MR^2 (2/3); Solid uniform sphere = 2/5 MR^2 (2/5); Thin rod (length L) about centre = ML^2/12, about end = ML^2/3.

Additional high-yield MOIs: Rectangular plate (sides a, b) about centre perp axis = M(a^2 + b^2)/12; Solid cone about symmetry axis = (3/10) M R^2; Triangular lamina (height h) about base = M h^2 / 6.
Parallel Axis Theorem (ALL 1D/2D/3D bodies): I_axis = I_cm + M d^2, where I_cm MUST pass through the Centre of Mass and be parallel to the target axis at separation d.

Perpendicular Axis Theorem (PLANAR laminae ONLY): I_z = I_x + I_y, where x, y lie strictly inside the lamina plane and z is perpendicular through their intersection. Example: Disc diameter I_d = (MR^2/2)/2 = MR^2/4; Ring diameter I_d = MR^2/2.

Cavity / Cutout MOI: Compute I_cavity about the SAME target axis using its own mass M_cav (remember Area ratio for 2D, Volume ratio for 3D!) and Parallel Axis Theorem if off-centre, then subtract: I_rem = I_full - I_cav.

Scaling invariance: If a uniform angular sector (angle theta) of a disc/ring of mass M and radius R is cut, its MOI about the centre axis stays IDENTICAL to full body formula (MR^2/2 for disc sector, MR^2 for ring sector) in terms of the sector's own mass M!

sections.heading: Torque, Rotational Equilibrium & Fixed-Axis Hinge Reactions
sections.summary: Torque tau = r x F drives angular acceleration alpha via tau_net = I alpha about a fixed axis or about the Centre of Mass. Sudden release of a hinged rod creates instantaneous hinge reaction forces governed by both COM linear acceleration and angular acceleration.
keyPoints: Vector torque: tau = r x F (magnitude r F sin theta = F * r_perp), direction by right-hand curl rule. Torque of a couple (equal, opposite forces separated by d) = F * d, completely independent of reference origin!
General rigid-body static equilibrium: BOTH Sum(F_ext) = 0 AND Sum(tau_ext) = 0 about any convenient pivot point (pick pivot where unknown forces intersect to eliminate them!).
Fixed-axis rotation dynamics: tau_hinge = I_hinge alpha; Rotational KE = (1/2) I_hinge omega^2; Rotational work W = integral(tau d theta); Power P = tau . omega.

Instantaneous hinge reaction on released horizontal rod (mass M, length L): Just after release, tau = Mg(L/2) = (ML^2/3) alpha => alpha = 3g / (2L). Tip accelerates at a_tip = alpha L = 1.5 g (> g!), while COM accelerates at a_cm = (3/4)g, so upward hinge force N = Mg - M(3g/4) = Mg/4!

Angular motion at arbitrary angle theta: Use energy conservation (1/2) I_hinge omega^2 = M g Delta h_cm to find omega(theta), then combine with radial equation F_hinge,rad - Mg sin theta = M omega^2 (L/2) for full hinge reaction.

sections.heading: Toppling vs Sliding Criteria & Normal Reaction Shift
sections.summary: An external horizontal push or incline gravity shifts the line of action of the Normal force N toward the leading edge to balance torque. A block topples before sliding whenever the required stabilizing shift exceeds half the base width before static friction reaches mu_s N.
keyPoints: Physical mechanism of toppling: Normal reaction is distributed across the base; as tipping torque grows, N shifts forward until it acts purely at the front edge corner (distance b/2 from COM).

Uniform block (width b, height h, pushing force F at height y above floor): Sliding starts at F_slide = mu_s mg. Taking torque about front edge: F y = mg (b/2) => toppling starts at F_topple = mg b / (2 y).
Toppling before sliding condition: F_topple < F_slide <=> b / (2 y) < mu_s, i.e., mu_s > b / (2 y). For force at top of uniform cube (y = h = b): topples if mu_s > 0.5.

Block on rough inclined plane (base width b, height h, angle theta): Normal shifts to lower corner at tan(theta) = b / h. Sliding starts at tan(theta) = mu_s. Therefore, block TOPPLES before sliding if mu_s > b / h (for a cube b = h, topples if mu_s > 1).
Zero-work note during pure tipping: Until corner lifts, friction at pivot edge does zero work.

sections.heading: Pure Rolling Kinematics & Dynamics on Flat & Inclined Surfaces
sections.summary: Pure rolling enforces zero relative velocity between the wheel's bottom contact point and the supporting surface: v_cm = omega R and a_cm = alpha R. Because the contact point is instantaneously at rest, static friction does ZERO work during pure rolling, conserving total mechanical energy.
keyPoints: Velocity field in pure rolling (ground rest): Bottom point v_B = 0 (ICOR); COM v_C = omega R; Topmost point v_T = 2 v_cm; Horizontal side points = sqrt(2) v_cm at 45 deg; general rim point at angle theta from bottom has speed 2 v_cm sin(theta/2).
Rolling energy partition: K_total = K_trans + K_rot = (1/2) M v_cm^2 [1 + k^2/R^2]. Fraction translational = 1 / (1 + k^2/R^2); fraction rotational = (k^2/R^2) / (1 + k^2/R^2).

Pure rolling down rough incline (angle theta): a = g sin(theta) / (1 + k^2/R^2). Race ranking from rest (fastest to slowest): Solid Sphere (5/7) > Disc/Solid Cylinder (2/3) > Hollow Sphere (3/5) > Ring/Hollow Cylinder (1/2) > Sliding frictionless block (1, wins overall!).

Friction force & minimum mu for pure rolling down incline: f_s = M g sin(theta) * [k^2/R^2 / (1 + k^2/R^2)] acting UP the incline! Minimum friction coefficient required: mu_min = tan(theta) / (1 + R^2/k^2). Notice ring needs (tan theta)/2, solid sphere needs only (2/7) tan theta!

Applied horizontal force F at height h above ground on flat rough surface (centre at R): Taking torque about bottom contact gives a = F h / [M R (1 + k^2/R^2)]. Static friction vanishes strictly at the sweet spot h = R + k^2/R, acts BACKWARD when F pulls below it (e.g., at COM h = R), and acts FORWARD when F pulls above it!

sections.heading: Angular Momentum Conservation & Rigid-Body Collisions
sections.summary: Total angular momentum about any stationary origin O combines orbital COM angular momentum and spin about COM: L_O = r_cm x (M v_cm) + I_cm omega. Whenever net external torque about O vanishes, L_O remains strictly conserved even across inelastic impacts and internal rearrangements.
keyPoints: General angular momentum vector: L_O = r_cm x (M v_cm) + I_cm omega. Choose axis O carefully: for pure rotation about fixed hinge, L_hinge = I_hinge omega; for free planar body, add orbital + spin terms with consistent CW/CCW signs!
Newton's 2nd Law for rotation: tau_ext,O = dL_O / dt (valid for fixed O, COM, or O moving parallel to v_cm!).

Internal rearrangement (Ice skater / Turntable / Bug walking on disc): When I changes via internal radial forces (zero external torque), I1 omega1 = I2 omega2, while KE changes by Delta K = (1/2) L^2 (1/I2 - 1/I1) due to internal work!

Bullet/clay hitting hinged rod: Hinge exerts huge unknown impulse during collision, so linear momentum is NOT conserved! Conserve angular momentum strictly ABOUT THE HINGE (since hinge impulse has zero moment arm): m v d = (I_rod + m d^2) omega.

Particle hitting FREE rod on smooth table: Both linear momentum P AND angular momentum L about system COM (or about any fixed table point) are conserved! Combine with restitution e along normal at impact point.

sections.heading: Combined Translation + Rotation & Angular Impulse
sections.summary: When an impulse J strikes a free rigid body off-centre, it simultaneously alters COM linear momentum (J = M Delta v_cm) and spin angular momentum (r x J = I_cm Delta omega). Locating the exact impact height where bottom velocity stays zero gives the zero-slip sweet spot.
keyPoints: Linear + Angular impulse pair: J = M (v_f - v_i) and r_imp x J = I_cm (omega_f - omega_i). For billiard cue strike at height h_0 above centre of sphere/cylinder: J h_0 = I_cm omega and J = M v_cm => immediate pure rolling (v_cm = omega R) requires h_0 = I_cm / (M R) = k^2 / R above centre (i.e., 2R/5 above centre for solid sphere!).

Work-Energy in sliding-to-rolling transition on rough floor: Kinetic friction does negative net work W_f = Delta K_trans + Delta K_rot < 0 until v_cm = omega R, while angular momentum about the ground line remains conserved.
Kinetic energy of general planar rigid body: K = (1/2) M v_cm^2 + (1/2) I_cm omega^2 = (1/2) I_ICOR omega^2 instantaneously.
In pure rolling on flat ground at constant speed v_cm, friction is ZERO (no tendency to slip unless accelerated!).

Directional slip check during rolling + sliding: Contact point velocity v_contact = v_cm - omega R (for CW forward roll); if v_contact > 0, forward slip occurs so kinetic friction acts BACKWARD; if v_contact < 0 (overspin), kinetic friction acts FORWARD!

derivationsAndGraphs.title: Incline Rolling Acceleration & Kinetic Energy Partition
derivationsAndGraphs.expressionOrCurve: a = g sin(theta) / (1 + k^2/R^2) ; K_rot / K_total = (k^2/R^2) / (1 + k^2/R^2)
derivationsAndGraphs.keyTakeaway: Smaller shape factor k^2/R^2 puts more energy into translation and wins the incline race: Solid sphere (2/5) > Disc (1/2) > Hollow sphere (2/3) > Ring (1).

derivationsAndGraphs.title: Speed Profile Around a Pure Rolling Wheel (ICOR Geometry)
derivationsAndGraphs.expressionOrCurve: v(theta) = 2 v_cm sin(theta / 2)  (theta measured from bottom contact point)
derivationsAndGraphs.keyTakeaway: Bottom = 0, side (90 deg) = sqrt(2) v_cm, top (180 deg) = 2 v_cm. Acceleration of bottom contact is NOT zero — it is v_cm^2/R = omega^2 R strictly UPWARD!

traps: Perpendicular Axis Theorem I_z = I_x + I_y is STRICTLY for thin planar laminae! Using it on a 3D sphere or cylinder gives completely wrong answers.
Parallel Axis Theorem trap: NEVER jump from axis A to axis B via I_B = I_A + M d^2 unless A passes strictly through the Centre of Mass! Go A -> COM -> B.
Incline friction trap: Rolling friction f_s is NOT mu_s N! It takes only the required static value M g sin(theta) / (1 + R^2/k^2) up to mu_s N.
Sliding block vs rolling sphere race: A frictionless sliding block (a = g sin theta) ALWAYS beats a pure rolling solid sphere (a = 5/7 g sin theta)!
Hinge impact momentum trap: When a bullet hits a hinged rod, linear momentum is NOT conserved because the hinge delivers an external impulse! Always conserve L ABOUT THE HINGE.
Uniform flat-ground rolling friction: If a sphere rolls at constant velocity on a horizontal floor, static friction is ZERO (not mu mg!).

Derive cavity MOI for a disc with an eccentric hole using Area scaling and Parallel Axis Theorem.

Derive pure rolling incline acceleration a = g sin theta / (1 + k^2/R^2) and minimum mu.
Verify sweet-spot height h_above_cm = k^2/R where horizontal impulse causes instant pure rolling with zero friction.

solvedExamples.question: Find the Moment of Inertia of a uniform disc of mass M and radius R about a tangent lying IN the plane of the disc.
steps: About central perpendicular axis (z): I_z = (1/2) M R^2.
By Perpendicular Axis Theorem for planar disc (I_x = I_y = I_diam): 2 I_diam = I_z => I_diam = (1/4) M R^2.
A tangent in the plane is parallel to a diameter at separation d = R.
Apply Parallel Axis Theorem: I_tangent = I_diam + M R^2 = (1/4) M R^2 + M R^2 = (5/4) M R^2.
solvedExamples.pitfall: Adding MR^2 to I_z (giving 3/2 MR^2, which is tangent PERPENDICULAR to the plane) instead of I_diam!

solvedExamples.question: A uniform solid cylinder of mass M and radius R rolls without slipping down an inclined plane of angle 30 deg. Find its linear acceleration and the minimum coefficient of static friction required (g = 10 m/s^2).
steps: For solid cylinder, k^2 / R^2 = 1/2.
Required static friction: f_s = I_cm (a / R^2) = (1/2) M a = M g sin(30) / 3 = M(5)/3.
Require f_s <= mu_min N = mu_min M g cos(30) => mu_min = tan(30) / (1 + 2) = (1 / sqrt(3)) / 3 = 1 / (3 sqrt(3)) ~ 0.192.
solvedExamples.pitfall: Setting f_s = (1/2) M g sin(30) by forgetting to divide by (1 + R^2/k^2) = 3!

solvedExamples.question: A solid sphere, a hollow sphere, and a disc of equal mass and radius are released simultaneously from rest at the top of a rough incline and roll purely. Which reaches the bottom first, and what is the ratio of their final COM speeds at the bottom?
steps: At vertical drop H, energy conservation gives M g H = (1/2) M v^2 (1 + k^2/R^2) => v = sqrt(2 g H / (1 + k^2/R^2)).
Shape factors (1 + k^2/R^2): Solid sphere = 7/5 = 1.4; Disc = 3/2 = 1.5; Hollow sphere = 5/3 ~ 1.67.
Since acceleration and final speed are both largest for smallest (1 + k^2/R^2), Solid Sphere reaches the bottom FIRST.
Speed ratio v_ss : v_disc : v_hs = sqrt(5/7) : sqrt(2/3) : sqrt(3/5).
solvedExamples.answer: Solid Sphere first ; v ratio = sqrt(5/7) : sqrt(2/3) : sqrt(3/5)
solvedExamples.pitfall: Assuming all reach simultaneously because mass M cancels, forgetting rotational inertia k^2/R^2!

solvedExamples.question: A uniform thin rod of mass M = 3 kg and length L = 1 m is pivoted smoothly at its top end and hangs vertically at rest. A horizontal clay ball of mass m = 1 kg moving at v = 10 m/s hits the lower end of the rod and sticks to it. Find the angular velocity just after impact and the maximum angle theta turned by the rod (g = 10 m/s^2).
steps: During impact, hinge exerts impulsive reaction, so conserve L about the top hinge: L_i = m v L = 1 x 10 x 1 = 10 kg.m^2/s.
Combined MOI about hinge: I_sys = M L^2 / 3 + m L^2 = 3(1)/3 + 1(1) = 2 kg.m^2.
Angular velocity after impact: omega = L_i / I_sys = 10 / 2 = 5 rad/s.
Post-impact energy conservation (hinge does zero work): (1/2) I_sys omega^2 = [M g (L/2) + m g L] (1 - cos theta).
Substitute: 0.5(2)(25) = [3(10)(0.5) + 1(10)(1)] (1 - cos theta) => 25 = 25 (1 - cos theta) => cos theta = 0 => theta = 90 degrees!
solvedExamples.pitfall: Conserving linear momentum M_tot v_cm = m v (fails due to hinge impulse!) or forgetting the + m L^2 term in I_sys!
